newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives give candidates EMU freedom.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives give candidates EMU freedom.

text.p: The ruling Conservative Party told parliamentarians opposed to a single European currency on Wednesday it would not use strong-arm tactics to force them into toeing the party line in the imminent election campaign.

The assurance, given to a private meeting of legislators, is likely to mean that some 150 of the ruling party's 641 candidates will say in their election addresses to local voters that they oppose any move to jettison the pound sterling.
That would make it barely conceivable that a Conservative government could defy their stance and join other European Union countries in adopting the new currency in 1999.

The Conservatives have been split for years on the question of a single currency, with Prime Minister John Major adopting a wait-and-see attitude and refusing to yield to pressure from so-called Eurosceptics to rule out British participation.

Sir Marcus Fox, chairman of a committee which represents rank-and-file Conservative legislators, told the meeting he had approached party chairman Brian Mawhinney about rumours that the party was planning to edit candidates' election addresses.

"The party chairman has asked me to make the position absolutely clear -- there will be no censorship of the personal messages of colleagues," Fox told the meeting. "This has always been the case, and will remain so."
Fox read out the text of his remarks to reporters immediately after the meeting ended.
He said he coupled the no-censorship assurance with a plea to colleagues to do nothing at the election to prejudice the party's chances of a fifth consecutive election victory.
Last week, the cabinet moved towards the Eurosceptic line by declaring it was unlikely that the currency would go ahead in 1999 and unlikely that Britain would take part if it did.
The Conservatives' reluctant agreement to allow candidates to go their own way on a single currency contrasts with a hard line by opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair.

He said at the weekend he would not accept "personal manifestos" by the party's candidates in the coming poll. "I do not believe you can have a group of candidates effectively standing on a separate manifesto," Blair said in an interview.

Labour, almost 20 points ahead of the Conservatives in the opinion polls with an election due by May 22, has also refused to commit itself on European economic and monetary union, but has generally taken a more sympathetic view on the idea.
